seo_title: What Is an Impasse in Insurance Appraisal? Texas Guide
meta_description: What is an impasse in insurance appraisal? Why appraisers deadlock, how umpires and Texas courts break the tie, and next steps.
h1: What Is an Impasse in Insurance Appraisal?
excerpt: What an impasse in insurance appraisal means, why appraisers deadlock, how an umpire or Texas court breaks the tie, and how owners keep claims moving.
key_takeaways: An impasse occurs when appraisers cannot agree on the amount of loss or on an umpire.
The umpire decides only disputed items; two signatures generally make the award.
Most Texas policies let a court appoint the umpire if appraisers cannot agree.
Scope, pricing, causation and weak documentation drive most impasses.
Signing partial agreements narrows the dispute and speeds resolution.
body_html:
An impasse in insurance appraisal happens when the two appraisers cannot agree on the amount of loss, or cannot even agree on an umpire. Under most Texas policies, an impasse sends the disputed items to a neutral umpire; if the appraisers cannot pick one, either side can usually ask a court to appoint the umpire.

Appraisal is designed to resolve claim disputes without a lawsuit, but it does not always go smoothly. Sometimes the two appraisers reach agreement quickly. Other times they stall over scope, pricing or causation, and the process seems to stop. Understanding what an appraisal impasse is, why it happens and what comes next helps Texas homeowners and commercial property owners keep their claims moving.

How does insurance appraisal work?

Most Texas homeowners and commercial property policies include an appraisal clause. When you and the carrier agree the damage is covered but disagree about the amount of loss, either side can usually demand appraisal in writing. Each party then selects a competent, disinterested appraiser, and the two appraisers select an umpire.

The appraisers inspect the property, exchange estimates and try to agree. If they do, they sign an award. If they cannot, they submit their differences to the umpire, and an award signed by any two of the three generally sets the amount of loss. Our page on what an insurance appraisal is covers the basics.

What is an impasse in insurance appraisal?

An impasse is the point where the appraisers stop making progress. It can happen at two stages:

  1. Umpire selection impasse: the two appraisers cannot agree on who should serve as umpire.
  2. Amount-of-loss impasse: the appraisers have exchanged estimates and negotiated but still disagree on some or all line items.

An impasse is not a failure of the process. It is a built-in step. The appraisal clause anticipates disagreement, which is why the umpire exists. Read what happens if appraisers disagree for a deeper look at the umpire stage.

Type of impasseWhat it looks likeTypical next step
Umpire selectionAppraisers reject each other's proposed umpiresEither side asks a court of record to appoint an umpire, as most Texas policies allow
Partial amount-of-lossAgreement on most items, disagreement on a fewAppraisers sign agreed items and submit the rest to the umpire
Full amount-of-lossEstimates remain far apart on major itemsEach appraiser presents its estimate and evidence to the umpire
Procedural stallOne side stops responding or delays inspectionWritten follow-up, firm deadlines, and possibly court involvement

Why do impasses happen during insurance appraisal?

Scope of damage disputes

The most common cause is disagreement about what needs to be repaired. One appraiser includes full roof replacement; the other includes repairs to two slopes. One includes drywall in three rooms; the other includes one. Scope disputes drive most large differences.

Pricing disagreements

Even with the same scope, appraisers can disagree on unit costs, labor rates, overhead and profit, or whether local market conditions justify adjustments to software pricing. After a major storm, labor and material costs can rise quickly, and one appraiser may rely on current supplier quotes while the other relies on standard price lists. Supplier invoices and documented local pricing help bridge that gap.

Causation disagreements

Was the damage caused by the storm on the date of loss, by an earlier event, or by wear and tear? Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), Texas appraisers can assess the cause and extent of damage as part of determining the amount of loss, but they cannot decide coverage. Causation questions often lead to impasse because they require judgment calls.

Weak documentation

When one side lacks photos, measurements or a line-item estimate, the other appraiser has little reason to move. Thin evidence makes impasses longer and outcomes less predictable, because the umpire has nothing concrete to weigh against the other side's estimate. See what evidence helps during insurance appraisal.

What are the signs an appraisal is reaching an impasse?

  • Repeated estimate rejections without specific, line-item reasons.
  • Long communication delays between appraisers.
  • Multiple reinspections that do not change either side's numbers.
  • Early talk of the umpire before real negotiation has happened.
  • Constant supplemental disputes as new items are added and contested.

What role does the umpire play during an impasse?

The umpire is a neutral third party who decides only the items the appraisers cannot agree on. Umpires review each appraiser's estimate, photos and supporting documents, may inspect the property and may ask questions. The umpire then sides with one appraiser on each disputed item or sets a value in between, depending on the evidence. Once the umpire and one appraiser sign, the award is generally final as to the amount of loss.

If the appraisers cannot agree on an umpire, most Texas policies allow either party to ask a judge of a court of record in the county where the property is located to select one. Learn more in how insurance umpires are chosen in Texas and on our umpire services page.

An illustrative example

Consider a hypothetical hail claim on a two-story home. The policyholder's appraiser includes full roof replacement, gutters and window screens. The carrier's appraiser agrees on gutters and screens but includes only three slopes of roofing. After negotiation, the appraisers sign off on gutters, screens and pricing, leaving one question: whether the remaining slopes have functional hail damage. The umpire reviews test-square photos for each slope, inspects the roof and decides that item. Instead of reopening the whole claim, the impasse was narrowed to a single, evidence-driven question.

Tip: Ask your appraiser to send agreed items to the other side in writing and sign a partial agreement where possible. Narrowing the dispute to a short list of items makes the umpire's job faster and keeps attention on the evidence that matters.

Why do Texas claims often reach appraisal impasse?

Texas sees frequent hail, wind, hurricane and freeze losses, often in waves that affect thousands of properties. Claims involving large roofs, multiple buildings or competing storm dates are especially prone to causation and scope disputes. Pricing also varies across the state; a repair in Houston may be priced differently than the same repair in Lubbock or El Paso.

Texas law adds structure. Chapter 542 of the Insurance Code governs prompt payment of claims, and the Texas Supreme Court's decisions in Barbara Technologies v. State Farm Lloyds and Ortiz v. State Farm Lloyds (both 2019) address how payment of an appraisal award affects prompt-payment and extra-contractual claims. If an impasse involves significant legal questions, talk with a Texas attorney. This is general information, not legal advice.

How does an appraisal impasse affect property owners?

Delays have real costs. Repairs may be postponed, temporary fixes can fail, and contractors may move on to other jobs. Interior damage can worsen, and businesses may lose income or tenants. The stress of an unresolved claim also takes a toll on families and owners.

Commercial owners feel additional pressure. Tenants may withhold rent or demand repairs, lenders may ask about the status of the claim, and business income losses can grow while the property waits for repairs. Multifamily and retail owners should keep tenants informed and document any operational impact.

Keep mitigating damage during appraisal, document the property's condition over time, and stay in regular contact with your appraiser so you know where the process stands.

Can an appraisal impasse be avoided?

Not always, but it can often be shortened or narrowed:

  • Thorough documentation from the start: photos, measurements, moisture readings and a complete documentation checklist.
  • Detailed inspections that cover every slope, room and component.
  • Line-item estimates in Xactimate or Symbility so differences are easy to pinpoint.
  • Professional communication between appraisers, focused on evidence rather than positions.
  • Experienced appraisers who understand construction, pricing and the Texas appraisal process.

Mistakes that make appraisal impasses worse

  • Waiting too long to invoke appraisal or to respond to the other side.
  • Accepting verbal explanations instead of written, line-item reasons.
  • Hiring an appraiser without estimating experience or real independence.
  • Ignoring the policy's appraisal clause, deadlines and umpire selection procedure.
  • Expecting the umpire to award every disputed item to your side.

What happens after an appraisal impasse is resolved?

Once the umpire and one appraiser sign the award, it generally sets the amount of loss. The carrier then applies the policy terms, subtracts the deductible and prior payments, and issues payment. On replacement cost policies, withheld depreciation may still be recoverable after repairs are completed; our recoverable depreciation calculator can help you estimate it.

Coverage questions that appraisers cannot decide remain open. If the carrier disputes coverage for part of the award, that issue may need to be resolved separately. Ask the carrier to explain in writing any portion of the award it does not intend to pay, and keep that letter with your claim records.

Next steps if your appraisal has stalled

  1. Review your policy's appraisal clause, especially umpire selection and timing.
  2. Ask your appraiser for a written list of agreed and disputed items.
  3. Strengthen evidence on the disputed items before they go to the umpire.
  4. If the appraisers cannot agree on an umpire, discuss court appointment.
  5. Keep realistic expectations and stay professional throughout; emotional arguments rarely persuade an umpire, while organized evidence does.
  6. Track costs, such as temporary repairs and additional living expenses, so nothing is forgotten when the award is paid.

faqs.q: What happens if appraisers cannot agree on an umpire?
faqs.a: Most Texas appraisal clauses allow either party to ask a judge of a court of record in the county where the property is located to select the umpire. The exact procedure and timing depend on your policy language, so review the clause and discuss court appointment with your appraiser if negotiations over the umpire stall.

faqs.q: How long does an appraisal impasse last?
faqs.a: It varies. A partial impasse that goes to an umpire may resolve within weeks, while a dispute over umpire selection that requires court appointment can add months. Strong documentation, partial agreements on undisputed items and prompt communication from both sides usually shorten the delay.

faqs.q: Does the umpire have to pick one appraiser's number?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Umpires review the evidence for each disputed item and may side with one appraiser or set a value in between, depending on the policy and the facts. The award becomes effective when the umpire and at least one appraiser sign it, which is why evidence on each disputed item matters.

faqs.q: Can I withdraw from appraisal if it reaches an impasse?
faqs.a: Generally, once appraisal is properly invoked under the policy, either side can ask a court to compel participation, so walking away is usually not a simple option. Withdrawing may also create legal complications. If you are considering it, speak with a Texas attorney about your specific situation.

faqs.q: Can an impasse be about causation?
faqs.a: Yes. Appraisers frequently disagree about whether damage came from the reported storm, an earlier event or wear and tear. Texas courts allow appraisers to assess causation as part of determining the amount of loss, but they cannot decide coverage. Weather data, prior photos and inspection reports help resolve causation disagreements.
